lead: Many useful problems ask for a ground state: the lowest energy of a molecule, or the best cut of a graph. A variational quantum algorithm guesses a state with a short circuit of adjustable angles, measures its energy, and lets a classical optimiser update the angles until the energy stops falling. The shallow circuit suits noisy hardware. VQE targets molecules and materials; QAOA targets combinatorial costs such as MaxCut.
prereq: You need eigenvalues and Hermitian matrices (Unit 1), measurement and expectation values (Unit 2), and rotation and CNOT circuits (Unit 3).

sections.h3: The variational principle gives an upper bound

blocks.text: A Hermitian H has real eigenvalues; call the smallest E₀. For any state |ψ⟩, the average energy is ⟨H⟩ = ⟨ψ|H|ψ⟩. The variational principle says ⟨H⟩ ≥ E₀, with equality only for a ground state. Expand |ψ⟩ = Σₖ cₖ|Eₖ⟩ in eigenvectors. Then ⟨H⟩ = Σₖ |cₖ|²Eₖ ≥ E₀ Σₖ |cₖ|² = E₀, because squared amplitudes sum to 1.

Every prepared state gives an upper bound. Push the bound down to approach E₀. The exact expectation ⟨H⟩ can never fall below E₀. A finite-shot estimate is random and can land on either side of the true value, which is why many shots are needed.

The state comes from an ansatz: a fixed circuit with angles θ = (θ₁, θ₂, …) preparing |ψ(θ)⟩ = U(θ)|0…0⟩. Hardware-efficient ansätze use layers of RY(θ) and CNOTs; problem-inspired ansätze copy the physics, such as unitary coupled cluster for a molecule. Write H = Σₖ hₖPₖ, where Pₖ is a tensor product of I, X, Y, Z and hₖ is real. Then ⟨H⟩ = Σₖ hₖ⟨Pₖ⟩, each ⟨Pₖ⟩ estimated from shots. Shot noise falls as 1/√S: 1000 shots give about 0.03 error per term; chemical accuracy is 0.0016 hartree.

blocks.where: θ are ansatz angles; hₖ and Pₖ are the coefficient and Pauli string of term k; ⟨Pₖ⟩ is its shot average; E₀ is the smallest eigenvalue of H.

blocks.text: Quantum phase estimation (see Unit 4) reads an eigenvalue of H into ancilla qubits. Started from a state with large overlap on the ground state, and with enough ancillas, it returns E₀ with high probability; poor overlap can return an excited energy. It needs long coherent circuits and fault tolerance. Grover search and amplitude amplification (see Unit 4) speed up search problems such as finding a marked solution; they are not alternatives for ground-state energy estimation. Both are out of reach on noisy hardware today.

sections.h3: The hybrid loop: optimiser, gradients, plateaus

items: Choose an ansatz and starting angles θ₀, often small random values.
Run the circuit and measure one Pauli term of H over many shots; repeat for each term.
Multiply each average by its coefficient and add to estimate ⟨H⟩.
Give the estimate to a classical optimiser; it returns new angles θ.
Repeat until the energy changes by less than a tolerance; report θ* and E.

blocks.where: the parameter-shift rule, valid when θ enters as e^(−iθP/2) with P a Pauli. Each shifted value is a full batch of shots. It is exact for the analytic expectation; no finite-difference error.

blocks.text: COBYLA is derivative-free and copes with noise, so tutorials often start with it. SPSA estimates a gradient from two circuit evaluations whatever the parameter count, suiting wide noisy circuits. Parameter-shift gradient descent is common when the shot budget allows it.

Barren plateaus: for random hardware-efficient ansätze the gradient of ⟨H⟩ shrinks exponentially with qubit count, so the optimiser stalls on a flat landscape rather than a minimum. Local cost functions, structured ansätze and informed initialisation help.

H₂ in a minimal basis has four spin orbitals, so four qubits in principle. Symmetry cuts it to 2 qubits after the Jordan–Wigner mapping. The electronic Hamiltonian has six Pauli terms: H = c₀I + c₁Z₀ + c₂Z₁ + c₃Z₀Z₁ + c₄X₀X₁ + c₅Y₀Y₁, with coefficients computed classically at the chosen bond length.

The ansatz is a few layers of RY on both qubits and a CNOT between them, so four or six angles (two per layer). Z terms are read directly. X₀X₁ needs H on both qubits before measurement; Y₀Y₁ needs S† then H on both. Each term gets its own shots.

Near equilibrium bond length 0.74 Å the exact ground energy in this basis is about −1.14 hartree. Hartree–Fock sits roughly 0.02 hartree higher; that difference is the correlation energy VQE recovers. Repeating at many bond lengths gives the potential curve; its minimum gives bond length and dissociation energy. Each extra spatial orbital adds qubits.

MaxCut splits vertices into two sets so as many edges as possible cross. Write vertex spin zᵢ ∈ {+1, −1}; edge (i,j) is cut when zᵢ ≠ zⱼ, indicator (1 − zᵢzⱼ)/2. Replacing zᵢ by Zᵢ gives H_C = Σ over edges (1 − ZᵢZⱼ)/2. Its eigenvalues are cut sizes, so QAOA maximises ⟨H_C⟩, equivalently minimises −H_C.

Start in |+⟩^⊗n, H on every qubit. Then p alternating layers: cost unitary U_C(γ)=e^(−iγH_C), a ZZ rotation on each edge; mixer U_X(β)=e^(−iβH_X) with H_X=ΣᵢXᵢ, one rotation per qubit. The 2p angles γ=(γ₁…γ_p), β=(β₁…β_p) are variational parameters; their count does not grow with the graph.

Each ⟨ZᵢZⱼ⟩ is estimated from shots and summed for the classical optimiser. Report approximation ratio r = ⟨H_C⟩ ÷ C_max ≤ 1, where C_max is the largest cut. Even p=1 guarantees a ratio comfortably above ½ on 3-regular graphs; larger p approaches 1. QAOA is a special case of the quantum alternating operator ansatz, where the mixer fits constraints instead of being a plain X sum.

figure.caption: The loop every variational algorithm runs: re-execute the parameterised circuit with new angles until the measured energy stops falling.

spec.title: Hybrid variational loop
spec.aria: A loop in which a parameterised circuit is run, its energy measured, and the angles updated by a classical optimiser until the energy stops falling.

examples.question: One qubit starts in |0⟩. RY(θ) prepares |ψ(θ)⟩ = cos(θ/2)|0⟩ + sin(θ/2)|1⟩, and H = Z. (a) Write ⟨H⟩(θ). (b) Find θ minimising it and the state. (c) Check the bound. (d) If 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2, give the best energy and gap to E₀. (e) What does shot noise add?
steps: Z|0⟩ = +|0⟩ and Z|1⟩ = −|1⟩, so H = Z has eigenvalues +1, −1; E₀ = −1, ground state |1⟩.
cos θ is smallest at θ = π, giving −1. The state is cos(π/2)|0⟩ + sin(π/2)|1⟩ = |1⟩.
The bound is tight here. For every θ, cos θ ≥ −1.
On 0 ≤ θ ≤ π/2, cos θ falls from 1 to 0; best is 0 at θ = π/2, state |+⟩. Gap = 0 − (−1) = 1 energy unit.

With S = 100 shots, the standard deviation of measured ⟨Z⟩ is about 1/√100 = 0.1 energy unit. A finite-shot estimate is random and can land on either side of the true ⟨H⟩; more shots shrink noise but cannot remove the gap in (d).
examples.answer: ⟨H⟩ = cos θ, minimised at θ = π with −1 energy unit = E₀, so the bound is tight; restricting θ to [0, π/2] leaves a gap of 1 energy unit.
examples.check:
import math

def energy(theta):
    return math.cos(theta / 2) ** 2 - math.sin(theta / 2) ** 2

print(round(energy(math.pi), 6))
print(round(energy(math.pi / 2), 6))
print(round(energy(math.pi / 2) - energy(math.pi), 6))

traps: Treating the optimiser's output as exact. The variational principle promises only ⟨H⟩ ≥ E₀; a weak ansatz or local minimum leaves a gap no extra shots can close.
Sign slip in MaxCut: H_C = Σ (1 − ZᵢZⱼ)/2 is maximised. Its ground state is the worst cut, not the best one.

Believing the parameter-shift rule is a finite difference. It uses two runs at θ ± π/2 and gives the exact derivative of the analytic expectation value; only shot noise is left, not a finite-difference approximation error.
Mixing up the two algorithms. VQE minimises a Hamiltonian energy from chemistry or physics; QAOA alternates a cost unitary with a mixer and is a special case of the alternating operator ansatz.
Forgetting basis changes. X and Y Pauli terms must be measured after H or S†H rotations; reading them in the Z basis gives a meaningless number.

quiz.q: State the variational principle and name the quantity it bounds.
quiz.a: For any state |ψ⟩ and Hermitian H with smallest eigenvalue E₀, ⟨ψ|H|ψ⟩ ≥ E₀. It bounds E₀ from above.

quiz.q: Why write H as a sum of Pauli strings, and how is ⟨H⟩ built?
quiz.a: Pauli strings have eigenvalues ±1 and are easy to measure. Linearity gives ⟨H⟩ = Σₖ hₖ⟨Pₖ⟩; each ⟨Pₖ⟩ is shot-averaged after any basis rotation, then weighted and summed.

quiz.q: What is a barren plateau and why does it matter?
quiz.a: For random deep ansätze the gradient of ⟨H⟩ falls exponentially with qubit count, so the landscape is nearly flat and the optimiser cannot choose a direction. Training cost grows exponentially unless local costs, structured ansätze or good initialisation are used.

quiz.q: Using |ψ(θ)⟩ = cos(θ/2)|0⟩ + sin(θ/2)|1⟩ and H = Z, evaluate ⟨H⟩ at θ = π/2 and θ = 0.
quiz.a: ⟨H⟩ = cos θ. At θ = π/2, ⟨H⟩ = 0 (state |+⟩). At θ = 0, ⟨H⟩ = 1 (state |0⟩). Both are ≥ E₀ = −1.

quiz.q: A 4-cycle graph 1-2-3-4-1 is solved by QAOA. Write H_C, state C_max, and give r for ⟨H_C⟩ = 3.
quiz.a: H_C = (1 − Z₁Z₂)/2 + (1 − Z₂Z₃)/2 + (1 − Z₃Z₄)/2 + (1 − Z₄Z₁)/2. The best cut scores 4, so C_max = 4 and r = 3/4 = 0.75.

quiz.q: A VQE run gives 2000 shots per Pauli term and standard deviation 0.02. How many shots give 0.005?
quiz.a: Error scales as 1/√S. To divide the error by 4, multiply shots by 16: S = 2000 × 16 = 32000 shots.

quiz.q: Compare VQE with quantum phase estimation for a molecular ground energy on today's hardware.
quiz.a: Quantum phase estimation (QPE; see Unit 4) reads an eigenvalue of H into ancillas. With large ground-state overlap and enough ancillas it returns E₀ with high probability; poor overlap can return an excited energy. It needs long coherent circuits and fault tolerance. VQE uses a short parameterised circuit plus repeated measurement and a classical optimiser, suiting noisy devices. Its price is an upper bound only: ansatz limits, local minima or shot noise can leave it above E₀; QPE avoids that but demands fault tolerance.

beyond: Not for the exam. ADAPT-VQE grows the circuit one operator at a time, keeping terms that lower the energy. Grouping commuting Pauli terms and classical shadows cut the shot bill. Error mitigation—zero-noise extrapolation, readout correction—sits between hardware and optimiser. Search next for ADAPT-VQE, qubit-ADAPT, parameter-shift rule and barren plateau mitigation.
